ety.text: From Middle English body, bodi, bodiȝ, from Old English bodiġ, bodeġ (“body, trunk, chest, torso, height, stature”), from Proto-West Germanic *bodag (“body, trunk”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰewdʰ- (“to be awake, observe”). Cognate with Old High German botah (“body, corpse, trunk, torso”) (whence Swabian Bottich (“body, torso”), Bavarian Bottich (“body, torso, carcass; lower part of a shirt or jacket”)).

senses.d: The physical structure of a human or animal seen as one single organism.
ex: I saw them walking from a distance, their bodies strangely angular in the dawn light.

senses.d: The fleshly or corporeal nature of a human, as opposed to the spirit or soul.
ex: The body is driven by desires, but the soul is at peace.

senses.d: A corpse.
ex: Her body was found at four o’clock, just two hours after the murder.
The bodies of 19-year-old best friends Holly Bowles and Bianca Jones were returned to Australia on Tuesday night.

senses.d: A murder.
ex: His gun had two bodies on it.
He caught a body and got forty years in prison.

senses.d: A person.
ex: Indeed, if it belonged to a poor body, it would be another thing; but so great a lady, to be sure, can never want it […]
What’s a body gotta do to get a drink around here?

senses.d: A human being, regarded as marginalized or oppressed.
ex: the early modern English husband not only took control over his wife's property upon marriage, he also acquired property in her body.
In doing so, Haritaworn also rethinks the marginality of transgender bodies and practices in queer movements and spaces.

senses.d: The torso, the main structure of a human or animal frame excluding the extremities (limbs, head, tail).
ex: The boxer took a blow to the body.

senses.d: The largest or most important part of anything, as distinct from its appendages or accessories; (of vehicles, sometimes) the outer shell (as contrasted with the frame and powertrain).
ex: The bumpers and front tyres were ruined, but the body of the car was in remarkable shape.

senses.d: The section of a dress extending from the neck to the waist, excluding the arms.
ex: Penny was in the scullery, pressing the body of her new dress.

senses.d: The content of a letter, message, or other printed or electronic document, as distinct from signatures, salutations, headers, and so on.
To give body or shape to something.
To construct the bodywork of a car.
To embody.
ex: I don’t say, one bodies the other / One’s spiritual truth; / But I do say it’s hard to lose either, / When you have both.

senses.d: To murder someone.
To utterly defeat someone.
ex: I keep getting bodied by kids half my age.

ex: You are a mere spirit, and have no knowledge of the bodily part of us.

senses.d: Real; actual; put into execution.
ex: Be brought to bodily act.

senses.d: In bodily form; physically, corporally.

senses.d: Pertaining to the whole body or mass; wholly.
ex: The papering of one side of the room had dropped down bodily, with fragments of plaster adhering to it, and almost blocked up the door.
